laws.title: Mobile Phone Use While Driving — Prohibited
laws.subtitle: Road Rules 2014 (NSW) — Handheld use banned; hands-free permitted
laws.fullDescription: New South Wales prohibits use of handheld mobile phones while driving. NSW uses a demerit point system; 4 demerit points for mobile phone use while driving. Hands-free operation via Bluetooth or dashboard mount is permitted.
laws.penalty: $349 fine + 4 demerit points (first offence). School/work zone: higher penalties.
exceptions: Hands-free (mounted or Bluetooth)
Emergency calls to 000
Emergency services on duty
laws.sourceLabel: New South Wales Road Rules

quiz.q: What is the fine for using a handheld mobile phone while driving in New South Wales?
quiz.explanation: In New South Wales, using a handheld mobile phone while driving attracts a fine of $349 and 4 demerit points.

laws.title: Recreational Fishing Licence — Licence required
laws.subtitle: Fisheries Management Act 1994 (NSW) — Recreational Fishing Fee required
laws.fullDescription: New South Wales: NSW requires a Recreational Fishing Fee (RFF) for most saltwater and freshwater fishing. Bag and size limits apply to most species. Commercial fishing requires separate licensing.
laws.penalty: Fishing without a fee/licence: infringement notice $50–$500; serious offences up to $44,000.
exceptions: Children under certain ages may be exempt
Fishing in exempted waters
Indigenous peoples exercising traditional fishing rights
laws.sourceLabel: New South Wales Fisheries

quiz.q: Is a recreational fishing licence required in New South Wales?
options: No — fishing is free in NSW
Yes — a licence/fee is required for most fishing
quiz.explanation: NSW requires payment of the Recreational Fishing Fee to fish in most waters.

laws.title: Drink Driving — 0.05 BAC Limit
laws.subtitle: Road Transport Act 2013 (NSW) — BAC ≥ 0.05 is illegal for most drivers
laws.fullDescription: Australia harmonised its drink-driving limit at 0.05% BAC in 1992. New South Wales enforces this through Random Breath Testing (RBT). Zero BAC applies to learner and P-plate (provisional) drivers and heavy vehicle operators. NSW operates high-volume RBT with police authorised to stop any vehicle.
laws.penalty: Mid-range DUI (0.08–0.149): min. 6 months disqualification, fine up to $2,200 (first). High-range (0.15+): up to 18 months disqualification, fine up to $3,300 and possible imprisonment.
exceptions: Full licence holders: 0.05% limit
Learner/P-plate drivers: 0.00% (zero BAC)
Commercial/bus/truck drivers: 0.00%
laws.sourceLabel: Road Transport Legislation

quiz.q: What is the general blood alcohol limit for fully licensed drivers in Australia?
quiz.explanation: Australia's drink-driving limit for fully licensed drivers is 0.05% BAC — lower than the US/Canada 0.08%. Learner and provisional drivers must have 0.00%.

laws.title: Open Alcohol in Vehicles
laws.subtitle: Road Transport Act 2013 (NSW) — No open liquor in vehicle
laws.fullDescription: New South Wales prohibits consuming alcohol in a motor vehicle and carrying open alcohol containers accessible to the driver or passengers while driving. NSW prohibits a person from driving or being in charge of a vehicle while consuming alcohol.
laws.penalty: Fine up to $2,200.
exceptions: Sealed containers may be transported in the boot
Passengers in licensed bus/limo services
Stationary vehicle in permitted location
laws.sourceLabel: New South Wales Liquor Act

quiz.q: Where must open alcohol be stored when travelling in a vehicle in New South Wales?
options: It is always prohibited to carry alcohol
quiz.explanation: Open alcohol accessible to driver or passengers is prohibited. Sealed containers stored in the boot are generally permitted.

laws.title: Recreational Cannabis — Illegal — criminal offence
laws.subtitle: Drug Misuse and Trafficking Act 1985 (NSW) — Illegal — small possession may result in diversion
laws.fullDescription: New South Wales: Recreational cannabis is illegal in NSW. Possession of up to 1 small quantity may be eligible for a cannabis cautioning program (first offence). Larger amounts face criminal charges. Cannabis remains prohibited under Commonwealth law (Criminal Code Act 1995) but state enforcement varies.
laws.penalty: Small quantity possession: caution (first) or up to 2 years/$2,200 (repeat). Supply: up to life imprisonment for large commercial quantities.
exceptions: Medical cannabis with TGA authorisation
ACT adults (personal use/cultivation only in ACT)
Hemp food products (federally permitted)
laws.sourceLabel: New South Wales Drug Laws / Commonwealth

quiz.q: What is the legal status of recreational cannabis in New South Wales?
quiz.explanation: Recreational cannabis is illegal in NSW. First-time possession of small amounts may receive a caution under the cannabis cautioning program.

laws.title: Medical Cannabis — TGA Federal Scheme
laws.subtitle: Therapeutic Goods Act 1989 (Cth) — TGA approval required
laws.fullDescription: Medical cannabis in Australia is federally regulated by the Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA). Patients need a prescription from an authorised prescriber or through the Special Access Scheme (SAS). Since 2016, TGA has approved thousands of practitioners and tens of thousands of patients. New South Wales follows the federal scheme.
laws.penalty: Possessing cannabis without valid authorisation: state drug law penalties apply.
exceptions: Authorised prescribers issue scripts directly
SAS-B allows practitioners to prescribe to specific patients
State/territory health departments may have additional rules
laws.sourceLabel: TGA (Therapeutic Goods Administration)

quiz.q: Which body regulates access to medical cannabis in Australia?
quiz.explanation: Medical cannabis is federally regulated in Australia by the TGA through the Special Access Scheme and Authorised Prescriber pathways.

laws.title: Firearms — National Firearms Agreement (NFA)
laws.subtitle: Firearms Act (state) + NFA 1996 — Strict licensing required
laws.fullDescription: Australia overhauled its firearm laws following the 1996 Port Arthur massacre. The National Firearms Agreement banned semi-automatic and pump-action rifles and shotguns. New South Wales: NSW has a firearms registry and strict Category A–H licensing system. Semi-automatics and pump-action shotguns (Categories C/D) banned except for farmers/occupational. All firearms require a licence and registration. A 28-day waiting period and genuine reason (sport/hunting/occupation) required.
laws.penalty: Unlicensed possession of a firearm: up to 14 years imprisonment (varies by state and firearm category).
exceptions: Licensed owners with genuine reason
Police and defence forces
Farmers for pest control (with licence)
laws.sourceLabel: New South Wales Firearms Act

quiz.q: What major event triggered Australia's strict National Firearms Agreement in 1996?
quiz.explanation: The Port Arthur massacre (35 killed, 23 wounded) in 1996 led Prime Minister Howard to introduce the NFA, which banned most semi-automatic weapons and led to a national buyback of 650,000+ firearms.

laws.title: Firearms Licence — Background Check & Safe Storage
laws.subtitle: Firearms Act 1996 (NSW) — Mandatory licence, check & storage
laws.fullDescription: All firearms owners in New South Wales must hold a valid firearms licence for each category of firearm they own. Police conduct background checks covering criminal history, domestic violence, and mental health. All firearms must be stored unloaded in an approved locked safe, separate from ammunition.
laws.penalty: Improper storage: licence suspension/cancellation, seizure of firearms, fines or imprisonment.
exceptions: Firearms clubs and ranges (supervised use)
Dealers must hold separate dealer's licence
Temporary permit for estates and inheritances
laws.sourceLabel: New South Wales Firearms Registry

quiz.q: How must firearms be stored in Australia?
options: Unloaded in a locked approved safe, ammo separate
In a vehicle for quick access
quiz.explanation: Australian law requires all firearms to be stored unloaded in an approved locked safe with ammunition stored separately — even in the owner's home.

laws.title: Self-Defence — Common Law & Criminal Code
laws.subtitle: Crimes Act 1900 (NSW) s. 418 — Proportionate force; no 'Stand Your Ground'
laws.fullDescription: Self-defence in New South Wales is governed by Crimes Act 1900 (NSW) s. 418. A person may use such force as is reasonably necessary to defend themselves or another. There is no 'Stand Your Ground' law in Australia — retreat is not legally required but is a factor courts consider. NSW codified self-defence in s. 418 of the Crimes Act. Excessive force where death results may be manslaughter.
laws.penalty: Excessive force negates the self-defence claim; charged as assault or more serious offence.
exceptions: Defending oneself from imminent unlawful force
Defending another person
Defence of property (with stricter limits)
laws.sourceLabel: New South Wales Criminal Code / Common Law

quiz.q: Does Australia have a 'Stand Your Ground' law like some US states?
options: No — proportional force is required; retreat not mandatory but considered
quiz.explanation: Australia has no Stand Your Ground doctrine. Self-defence requires proportionate force. Whether retreat was possible is one factor courts consider.

laws.title: Minimum Wage — National Minimum Wage
laws.subtitle: Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) s. 294 — Annual wage review
laws.fullDescription: Australia's National Minimum Wage (NMW) is set annually by the Fair Work Commission. As of July 2024, the NMW is $23.23/hour (or $882.80/week for a full-time worker). New South Wales workers are covered by the federal system under the Fair Work Act 2009. The National Minimum Wage applies to all states. Most workers in NSW are covered by awards which often exceed the NMW.
laws.penalty: Underpaying wages: Fair Work Ombudsman investigation, back-pay orders, civil penalties up to $18,780 per contravention (individual).
exceptions: Award rates apply in many industries and may exceed NMW
Enterprise agreements may set higher rates
Some state public servants covered by state employment laws
laws.sourceLabel: Fair Work Commission / Fair Work Act 2009

quiz.q: Who sets Australia's National Minimum Wage?
options: Fair Work Commission through annual review
quiz.explanation: The Fair Work Commission conducts an annual minimum wage review and sets the National Minimum Wage, which applies across Australia.

laws.title: Unfair Dismissal — Fair Work Act Protections
laws.subtitle: Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) Part 3-2 — Protection from unfair dismissal
laws.fullDescription: Unlike US at-will employment, Australia's Fair Work Act provides strong protection against unfair dismissal. Employees covered by the federal system who have completed the minimum employment period (1 year for small businesses, 6 months for others) may apply to the Fair Work Commission if dismissed harshly, unjustly, or unreasonably. NSW workers covered by the federal Fair Work Act enjoy unfair dismissal protections. Some NSW public servants remain under state industrial laws.
laws.penalty: Unfair dismissal remedy: reinstatement or compensation up to 26 weeks' pay (capped at half the high income threshold).
exceptions: Casual employees may have limited access (min 12 months regular service)
High-income employees above the threshold may have different options
Redundancy with genuine severance generally not unfair dismissal
laws.sourceLabel: Fair Work Act 2009 / Fair Work Commission

quiz.q: How long does an employee generally need to work before they can claim unfair dismissal in Australia?
quiz.explanation: The minimum employment period before a Fair Work Act unfair dismissal claim is 6 months (or 1 year if the employer has fewer than 15 employees).

laws.title: Union Rights & Industrial Action
laws.subtitle: Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) — Right to organise; protected industrial action
laws.fullDescription: The Fair Work Act protects employees' right to join unions, participate in union activities, and take protected industrial action during enterprise bargaining. New South Wales: NSW has a strong union history. The NSW Industrial Relations Commission handles state system workers (public servants). Federal Fair Work system applies to private sector. Unions are registered with the Fair Work Commission.
laws.penalty: Unprotected industrial action: injunctions, penalties. Employers cannot dismiss workers for union membership.
exceptions: Protected industrial action during bargaining — legal
Right of entry: union officials may enter workplaces with 24 hours notice
General protections: adverse action for exercising workplace rights is prohibited
laws.sourceLabel: Fair Work Act 2009

quiz.q: Can Australian employees take industrial action (e.g. strike) legally?
options: Yes — 'protected' industrial action during enterprise bargaining is legal
quiz.explanation: Protected industrial action during enterprise bargaining is legal under the Fair Work Act, provided notice and procedural requirements are met.

laws.title: Non-Compete Agreements
laws.subtitle: Common Law (Restraint of Trade) — Restraints must be reasonable
laws.fullDescription: Non-compete clauses in New South Wales are governed by Common Law (Restraint of Trade). Courts apply a reasonableness test — the restraint must go no further than necessary to protect the employer's legitimate business interests. NSW courts apply common law restraint of trade principles. Reasonableness of scope, duration, and area assessed. No statutory ban.
laws.penalty: Overly broad restraints struck down as unenforceable; employer may lose protection entirely.
exceptions: Non-solicitation of clients/employees more readily enforced
Sale-of-business restraints treated more leniently
Courts may 'read down' (reduce scope) rather than void entirely
laws.sourceLabel: New South Wales Contract Law

quiz.q: How do Australian courts treat overly broad non-compete clauses?
options: Void — non-competes are illegal in Australia
Scrutinised for reasonableness; overly broad clauses struck down or read down
Only enforceable if the employee was a senior executive
quiz.explanation: Australian courts apply a reasonableness test to non-competes and may 'read down' (reduce scope) or void clauses that go beyond what's necessary to protect legitimate interests.

laws.title: Paid Leave — Annual & Personal/Carer's Leave
laws.subtitle: Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) NES — Minimum leave entitlements
laws.fullDescription: The National Employment Standards (NES) under the Fair Work Act set minimum paid leave: 4 weeks annual leave per year, 10 days personal/carer's leave (sick leave) per year, and 2 days compassionate leave per occasion. These apply to full-time workers covered by the national system. NSW workers receive NES entitlements: 4 weeks annual leave, 10 days personal leave, long service leave (portable in some industries) after 5 years service.
laws.penalty: Underpaying leave: FWO back-pay orders, penalties.
exceptions: Part-time workers receive proportionate leave
Casual workers receive 25% casual loading instead
Awards and enterprise agreements may provide more generous leave
laws.sourceLabel: Fair Work Act 2009 / NES

quiz.q: How many days of paid personal/sick leave per year do full-time employees get under Australia's National Employment Standards?
quiz.explanation: The NES provides 10 days paid personal/carer's leave (sick leave) per year for full-time employees, accruing progressively.

laws.title: Unemployment Benefits — JobSeeker Payment
laws.subtitle: Social Security Act 1991 (Cth) — Federal JobSeeker
laws.fullDescription: Australia's unemployment support — JobSeeker Payment — is federally administered by Services Australia. As of 2024, the base rate is approximately $762.70/fortnight for singles (subject to income and assets tests). NSW residents access JobSeeker through Centrelink like all Australians. NSW's cost of living makes the payment particularly inadequate relative to local expenses. Australia has no province/state-level unemployment insurance system.
laws.penalty: Receiving incorrect payments: repayment required; fraud penalties under the Criminal Code.
exceptions: Mutual obligation requirements (job search activities) must be met
Income and assets tests reduce or eliminate payments for higher earners
Waiting periods may apply depending on circumstances
laws.sourceLabel: Services Australia / Social Security Act 1991

quiz.q: What is Australia's main unemployment payment called?
quiz.explanation: Australia's unemployment payment is called JobSeeker Payment (formerly Newstart Allowance), administered federally by Services Australia through Centrelink.

laws.title: Workers' Compensation — icare NSW (State Insurance Regulatory Authority)
laws.subtitle: Workers Compensation Act 1987 (NSW) — No-fault workplace injury scheme
laws.fullDescription: New South Wales's workers' compensation system provides no-fault coverage for workplace injuries and diseases. The scheme is administered by icare NSW (State Insurance Regulatory Authority). NSW workers' compensation is managed by icare and SIRA. The scheme provides income replacement and medical treatment. In exchange for coverage, injured workers generally cannot sue their employer.
laws.penalty: Employer failure to insure: fine up to $55,000.
exceptions: Self-employed workers not automatically covered
Some contractors may be workers under extended definitions
Comcare covers Commonwealth government employees
laws.sourceLabel: icare NSW (State Insurance Regulatory Authority)

quiz.q: What body administers workers' compensation in New South Wales?
quiz.explanation: New South Wales's workers' compensation is administered by icare NSW (State Insurance Regulatory Authority).

laws.title: Independent Contractors — Classification
laws.subtitle: Fair Work Act 2009 / Independent Contractors Act 2006 (Cth)
laws.fullDescription: Contractor vs employee classification in Australia is determined by multi-factor analysis (control, equipment, integration). The Fair Work Act 2009 (amended 2022) introduced a new 'employee-like' category and allows workers to challenge sham contracting arrangements. New South Wales: NSW applies the federal multi-factor test and the Independent Contractors Act 2006.
laws.penalty: Sham contracting (treating employees as contractors): civil penalties up to $93,900/contravention (company).
exceptions: Genuine business-to-business contractors retain independent status
Written contracts are one factor, not determinative
Digital platform workers ('gig economy') increasingly subject to employee-like protections
laws.sourceLabel: Fair Work Act 2009 / Independent Contractors Act 2006

quiz.q: What approach does Australia take to determine if someone is an employee or contractor?
options: Multi-factor 'real substance of the relationship' test
quiz.explanation: Australian courts apply a multi-factor test looking at the 'real substance' of the relationship, not just the written contract. Sham contracting is unlawful.

laws.title: Child Labour — Minimum Age & Restrictions
laws.subtitle: Children and Young Persons (Care and Protection) Act / Industrial Relations Act 1996 (NSW) — Children under 14 generally cannot work
laws.fullDescription: New South Wales: NSW permits light work (retail, hospitality) from age 14–15 with restrictions on hours. Full employment protections apply at 16. Federal NES restricts child labour in nationally regulated industries. Children must not work during school hours.
laws.penalty: Employing children under minimum age: significant fines.
exceptions: Entertainment industry with parental consent and permit
Family business (limited)
School-based apprenticeships with parental consent
laws.sourceLabel: New South Wales Employment Legislation

quiz.q: What is the general minimum working age in New South Wales?
quiz.explanation: In New South Wales, children generally must be at least 14 to work, with restrictions on hours and types of work for those under 18.

laws.title: Pay Equity — Fair Work Act & State Laws
laws.subtitle: Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) / Equal Opportunity legislation
laws.fullDescription: Pay equity in Australia is addressed through the Fair Work Commission's work value and minimum wage decisions, and through state/territory anti-discrimination and equal opportunity laws. New South Wales: NSW relies on the federal Fair Work system for pay equity. The NSW Government conducts pay equity assessments in the public sector. The gender pay gap in Australia is approximately 21.7% (2024, WGEA).
laws.penalty: Pay discrimination: complaints to Fair Work Commission or state equal opportunity body.
exceptions: Work value cases can result in pay rises for female-dominated industries
WGEA (Workplace Gender Equality Agency) reports on employer pay gaps
Enterprise bargaining must not discriminate
laws.sourceLabel: Fair Work Commission / New South Wales Equal Opportunity

quiz.q: Which federal agency publishes employer-level gender pay gap data in Australia?
quiz.explanation: Since 2024, WGEA has published employer-level gender pay gap data for organisations with 100+ employees — a world-leading transparency measure.

laws.title: Anti-Discrimination — Anti-Discrimination Act 1977 (NSW)
laws.subtitle: Anti-Discrimination Act 1977 (NSW) + federal Acts — Comprehensive protections
laws.fullDescription: New South Wales's Anti-Discrimination Act 1977 (NSW) prohibits discrimination in employment, goods/services, and accommodation on grounds including race, sex, disability, sexual orientation, gender identity, and more. Federal laws (Racial Discrimination Act, Sex Discrimination Act, Disability Discrimination Act, Age Discrimination Act) also apply. NSW prohibits discrimination on 19 grounds. NCAT (NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal) handles complaints.
laws.penalty: Complaints: state tribunal or Australian Human Rights Commission; remedies include compensation, apology, and policy changes.
exceptions: Genuine occupational requirements defence
Special measures (positive discrimination) to promote equality
Religious bodies may have limited exemptions in some states
laws.sourceLabel: New South Wales Anti-Discrimination / AHRC

quiz.q: Which body handles federal anti-discrimination complaints in Australia?
quiz.explanation: The Australian Human Rights Commission (AHRC) handles federal anti-discrimination complaints; state tribunals handle state-law complaints.

laws.title: Landlord Entry — Notice Required
laws.subtitle: Residential Tenancies Act 2010 (NSW) s. 72 — 24 hours notice required
laws.fullDescription: New South Wales requires landlords to give 24 hours written notice before entering a rental property for non-emergency purposes. NSW landlords must give at least 24 hours written notice before entering. Entry permitted 8 AM–8 PM on any day except Sunday and public holidays (except for urgent repairs).
laws.penalty: Illegal entry: NCAT complaint; potential compensation.
exceptions: Emergencies (flooding, fire, gas leak)
Tenant consents to immediate entry
Final inspection at end of tenancy with proper notice
laws.sourceLabel: New South Wales Residential Tenancies Act

quiz.q: How much notice must a landlord give before entering a rental property in New South Wales?
quiz.explanation: New South Wales requires 24 hours written notice before a landlord can enter a rental property (except for emergencies).

laws.title: Rental Bond — Maximum & Lodgement
laws.subtitle: Residential Tenancies Act 2010 (NSW) — Max bond: 4 weeks' rent (if rent ≤$700/wk) or unlimited (if rent >$700/wk); held by NSW Fair Trading (Rental Bonds Online)
laws.fullDescription: New South Wales: NSW rental bonds are lodged with NSW Fair Trading (Rental Bonds Online). Bonds must be lodged with NSW Fair Trading (Rental Bonds Online) (not held by the landlord) and returned within 14 days of tenancy ending.
laws.penalty: Bond withheld improperly: NCAT order.
exceptions: Bond returned if no claim within required period
Disputes handled by tribunal
Condition report at start prevents disputed claims
laws.sourceLabel: New South Wales Residential Tenancies / NSW Fair Trading (Rental Bonds Online)

quiz.q: Where must rental bonds be lodged in New South Wales?
quiz.explanation: In New South Wales, rental bonds must be lodged with NSW Fair Trading (Rental Bonds Online) — not held by the landlord or agent — to protect tenants.

laws.title: Rent Increases — No rent control — once per 12 months limit
laws.subtitle: Residential Tenancies Act 2010 (NSW) — No rent control; increases limited to once per 12 months
laws.fullDescription: New South Wales: NSW has no rent control — landlords may increase rent by any amount. However, rent can only be increased once every 12 months, and 60 days written notice is required.
laws.penalty: Rent increase without proper notice: tenant can challenge at NCAT.
exceptions: 60 days written notice required before any increase
Only one increase permitted per 12-month period
laws.sourceLabel: New South Wales Residential Tenancies

quiz.q: How often can a landlord increase rent in New South Wales?
options: No more than once every 12 months
quiz.explanation: NSW has no rent cap — landlords may raise rent any amount — but increases are limited to once per 12 months with 60 days' notice.

laws.title: Eviction — Notice & Tribunal Process
laws.subtitle: Residential Tenancies Act 2010 (NSW) — Formal process required; self-help eviction illegal
laws.fullDescription: New South Wales: NSW landlords must obtain a termination order from NCAT before a tenant can be evicted. Notice periods vary (14 days for non-payment to 90 days for no-grounds termination). Landlords cannot change locks, remove belongings, or cut off utilities to force a tenant out — these are illegal 'self-help' evictions.
laws.penalty: Illegal eviction: NCAT compensation order, criminal charge.
exceptions: Tenant can remedy breach before eviction order in many cases
Illegal eviction: tenant entitled to compensation and restoration of possession
Domestic violence provisions allow tenants to end lease safely
laws.sourceLabel: NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal (NCAT)

quiz.q: What is the correct legal process for a landlord to evict a tenant in Australia?
options: Applying to the state tribunal for a possession order
Calling police to remove the tenant
quiz.explanation: Landlords must obtain a formal possession order from the state tenancy tribunal. Self-help eviction (changing locks, removing possessions) is illegal in all Australian states.

laws.title: Short-Term Rentals (Airbnb/Stayz)
laws.subtitle: Environmental Planning and Assessment Act 1979 / local planning — Regulated by local council and state planning laws
laws.fullDescription: New South Wales: Short-term rentals in NSW are regulated through SEPP (Short-term Rental Accommodation) 2021. Properties in most areas can be listed for STR; Sydney has an 180-day cap for non-hosted stays in some zones.
laws.penalty: Non-compliance with SEPP: planning penalties.
exceptions: Primary residence (owner-occupied) may have different rules
Strata/body corporate rules may prohibit STR
GST registration required if STR income exceeds $75,000/year
laws.sourceLabel: New South Wales STR Regulations

quiz.q: Are short-term rentals regulated in New South Wales?
options: Regulated — registration, planning approval, or caps may apply
quiz.explanation: Short-term rentals in New South Wales are regulated — SEPP rules apply — Sydney caps non-hosted STR at 180 days in some zones.

laws.title: Land Tax — New South Wales
laws.subtitle: Land Tax Management Act 1956 (NSW) — Annual tax on unimproved land value
laws.fullDescription: New South Wales levies land tax annually on the total unimproved value of taxable land above a threshold. NSW land tax applies to total taxable land value over the threshold ($1,075,000 in 2024). Rate: 1.6% on value over threshold, 2% on value over $6,571,000. Principal place of residence is generally exempt. Land tax is a major revenue source for Australian states.
laws.penalty: Unpaid land tax: penalties, interest, and ultimately a charge on the land.
exceptions: Principal place of residence: exempt in most states
Primary production land: often exempt or concession
Trusts may lose exemptions on primary residence
laws.sourceLabel: New South Wales Revenue Office

quiz.q: Is the principal place of residence (family home) subject to land tax in New South Wales?
options: No — principal place of residence is generally exempt
Only if the land value exceeds $5M
quiz.explanation: In New South Wales, the principal place of residence is generally exempt from land tax. Investment properties and vacant land are taxed.

laws.title: Stamp Duty / Transfer Duty on Property
laws.subtitle: Duties Act 1997 (NSW) — Transfer duty applies
laws.fullDescription: New South Wales: NSW charges transfer duty (stamp duty) on property purchases. For a $1M property: approximately $40,335. Stamp duty (called transfer duty in some states) is a major upfront cost of purchasing property in Australia — typically 3–5% of the purchase price.
laws.penalty: Underpaying duty: penalty duty plus interest.
exceptions: First home buyer duty concessions — exemption/reduction up to $1M
Foreign buyers may pay additional surcharges
Commercial property may have different rates
laws.sourceLabel: New South Wales Revenue Office

quiz.q: What is stamp duty (transfer duty) in New South Wales?
options: A tax paid when purchasing real estate
A federal tax on all investments
quiz.explanation: Stamp duty is a state-based tax paid when purchasing real estate. In New South Wales, transfer duty applies — $40,335 on a $1M property.

laws.title: Income Tax — Federal Only (No State Income Tax)
laws.subtitle: Income Tax Assessment Act 1997 (Cth) — ATO administers
laws.fullDescription: Australia has no state or territory income taxes. All income tax is federal, administered by the Australian Taxation Office (ATO). Top marginal rate is 45% on income over $180,001 (plus 2% Medicare Levy). New South Wales residents are subject to federal income tax like all Australians. NSW residents pay federal income tax only; NSW has no state income tax.
laws.penalty: Tax evasion: civil penalties, criminal prosecution, up to 10 years imprisonment for serious fraud.
exceptions: Tax-free threshold: $18,200 (2024-25)
15% concessional rate on superannuation contributions
Capital gains discount: 50% for assets held over 12 months
laws.sourceLabel: Australian Taxation Office / Income Tax Assessment Act 1997

quiz.q: Does any Australian state or territory collect its own income tax?
options: Yes — all states have their own income tax
No — income tax is exclusively federal in Australia
Yes — states collect 10% of federal income tax
quiz.explanation: Unlike Canada or the US, Australia has no state income taxes. All income tax is collected by the federal ATO.

laws.title: GST — Goods and Services Tax (Federal 10%)
laws.subtitle: A New Tax System (Goods and Services Tax) Act 1999 (Cth) — 10% GST
laws.fullDescription: Australia's Goods and Services Tax (GST) is a federal 10% tax on most goods and services, introduced in July 2000 under the Howard government. GST revenue is distributed to the states and territories. NSW collects no GST directly — revenue distributed from federal pool to states. Most fresh food, health, education, and financial services are GST-free.
laws.penalty: Businesses must register if annual turnover exceeds $75,000 (or $150,000 for non-profits). Non-compliance: ATO audit, penalties.
exceptions: Fresh food (unprocessed) — GST-free
Health and medical services — GST-free
Educational courses — GST-free
Exports — GST-free (input tax credits available)
laws.sourceLabel: ATO / GST Act 1999

quiz.q: What is the rate of GST in Australia?
quiz.explanation: Australia's GST rate is 10%, introduced in 2000. Revenue is distributed to states and territories under the federal financial relations framework.

laws.title: Superannuation — Compulsory Retirement Savings
laws.subtitle: Superannuation Guarantee (Administration) Act 1992 (Cth) — 11% SGC
laws.fullDescription: Australia's superannuation system requires employers to contribute a percentage of an employee's earnings to a superannuation fund. The Superannuation Guarantee rate is 11% (2023-24), rising to 12% by 2025. NSW workers are entitled to SG contributions to their chosen super fund. Super is a key feature of Australian employment law and tax policy.
laws.penalty: Underpaying super: ATO SGC liability (rate plus interest plus admin fee), civil penalties, criminal prosecution for deliberate underpayment.
exceptions: Employees over 18 earning more than $450/month (threshold removed 2022 — all earnings now covered)
Self-employed may contribute voluntarily
Super funds must be licenced and regulated by APRA
laws.sourceLabel: ATO / Super Guarantee Act

quiz.q: What is the employer Superannuation Guarantee rate for 2023-24?
quiz.explanation: The Superannuation Guarantee rate is 11% for 2023-24, rising to 11.5% in 2024-25, and 12% from 2025-26.

laws.title: Smoke-Free Legislation — New South Wales
laws.subtitle: Smoke-free Environment Act 2000 (NSW) — Smoking banned in enclosed public spaces
laws.fullDescription: New South Wales bans smoking in all enclosed public spaces, workplaces, restaurants, and bars. NSW bans smoking in enclosed public places, outdoor dining areas, playgrounds, and within 10m of children's play equipment. Plain packaging of tobacco products has been federal law since 2012 (world-first). The minimum age for purchasing tobacco is 18.
laws.penalty: Individual: $300 fine. Business allowing smoking: up to $5,500.
exceptions: Outdoor dining areas may be smoke-free under local laws
Designated outdoor smoking areas where provided
Private residences (adults only)
laws.sourceLabel: New South Wales Smoke-Free Legislation

quiz.q: Australia was the first country in the world to introduce which tobacco control measure?

laws.title: Helmet Law — Mandatory for Cyclists
laws.subtitle: Road Rules 2014 (NSW) — Helmet compulsory for all cyclists
laws.fullDescription: New South Wales requires all cyclists to wear an approved helmet. Australia is unusual globally in mandating helmets for all cyclists of all ages (not just children). NSW requires all cyclists to wear an approved helmet. Fines apply for not wearing a helmet.
laws.penalty: No helmet: $344 fine.
exceptions: Helmet exemptions for medical reasons (rare, requires application)
Sikhs may be exempt in some states on religious grounds
E-scooter rules vary by jurisdiction

quiz.q: Is wearing a cycling helmet mandatory for adult cyclists in Australia?
options: No — only children must wear helmets
No — helmets are voluntary for adults
Yes — all cyclists must wear approved helmets
Only on roads, not shared paths

laws.title: Seatbelt Law — Mandatory for All Occupants
laws.subtitle: Road Rules 2014 (NSW) — All occupants must wear seatbelts
laws.fullDescription: New South Wales requires all vehicle occupants to wear seatbelts. NSW requires all vehicle occupants to wear seatbelts. Driver responsible for passengers under 16. The driver is responsible for ensuring passengers under 16 are correctly restrained. Approved child restraints are compulsory for children based on height/age.

exceptions: Medical exemption with certificate
Vehicles predating seatbelt requirements
Certain heavy vehicles, buses (if not fitted)

quiz.q: Who is responsible for ensuring child passengers are properly restrained in a vehicle in Australia?
quiz.explanation: The driver is legally responsible for ensuring all passengers under 16 are correctly restrained in an approved child restraint or seatbelt.

laws.title: Speed Limits — New South Wales
laws.subtitle: Road Rules 2014 (NSW) — Default: 50 urban / 110 highway
laws.fullDescription: New South Wales default speed limits: 50 km/h urban (default built-up area); 110 km/h on some motorways; 100 km/h other highways; 40 km/h school zones during school hours. Speed cameras (fixed and mobile) are widely used across Australia.
laws.penalty: Speeding: from $123 (up to 10 km/h over) to $2,530 (45+ km/h over). School zone: double demerit points.
exceptions: School zones: 40 km/h during school hours
Construction zones: reduced limits when workers present
Emergency vehicles exempt when responding
laws.sourceLabel: New South Wales Road Rules

quiz.q: What is the default speed limit in urban/built-up areas in New South Wales?
quiz.explanation: The default urban speed limit in New South Wales is 50 km/h. Highway limits are typically 110 km/h.

laws.title: Mobile Phone — Any Use Prohibited While Driving
laws.subtitle: Road Rules 2014 (NSW) — Holding a phone in any way while driving is illegal
laws.fullDescription: In New South Wales (and across Australia), any use of a handheld mobile phone while driving is illegal — including texting, checking notifications, scrolling, or holding the phone even at traffic lights or in slow-moving traffic. NSW police use phone detection cameras — AI-powered cameras that detect mobile phone use inside vehicles at highway speeds.
laws.penalty: $349 fine + 4 demerit points. Double demerit period: $698 + 8 demerit points.
exceptions: Hands-free (mounted, Bluetooth)
Emergency 000 calls
Parked with engine off (not stopped at lights)
laws.sourceLabel: New South Wales Road Rules

quiz.q: Can you briefly check a text at a red light in your car in Australia?
options: Yes — briefly is fine if not driving
No — handheld use is banned even when stopped at lights
quiz.explanation: Handheld mobile phone bans apply even when stopped at traffic lights in all Australian states and territories.

laws.title: Random Breath Testing (RBT) — Mandatory Compliance
laws.subtitle: Road Transport Act 2013 (NSW) — Police may stop any driver for RBT
laws.fullDescription: Random Breath Testing is legal and widely practised in New South Wales. Police can stop any vehicle at any time to conduct a breath test — no reasonable suspicion required. NSW operates the largest RBT program in Australia; millions of tests conducted annually. Australia pioneered RBT; Victoria introduced it in 1976.
laws.penalty: Refusal to submit to RBT: same or greater penalty as drink driving.
exceptions: Must stop when directed by police
Cannot refuse a breath test
Second test on a machine at the station if positive on roadside

quiz.q: Can Australian police conduct a Random Breath Test (RBT) without suspecting the driver of drink driving?
options: Yes — any driver can be stopped at any time for RBT
quiz.explanation: RBT is a cornerstone of Australian road safety. Police can stop any vehicle at any time and require a breath test — no suspicion needed. Refusal is an offence.

laws.title: Keep Left / Move Over — Emergency Vehicles
laws.subtitle: Road Rules 2014 (NSW) — Slow down and move over for emergency vehicles
laws.fullDescription: New South Wales requires drivers to move left and slow to 40 km/h (or less) when passing police, ambulance, fire, or breakdown vehicles with lights/sirens activated. Must slow to 40 km/h when emergency vehicle is stationary with lights activated.
laws.penalty: Failure to slow: $448 fine + 3 demerit points.
exceptions: Applies to all emergency and breakdown vehicles with lights activated
If safe lane change not possible, slow to well below speed limit
laws.sourceLabel: New South Wales Road Rules

quiz.q: What speed must drivers slow to when passing a stationary emergency vehicle with lights on in Australia?
quiz.explanation: The 'slow down, move over' rule in Australia requires drivers to slow to 40 km/h when passing stationary emergency or breakdown vehicles with lights activated.

laws.title: Speeding Penalties — New South Wales
laws.subtitle: Road Rules 2014 (NSW) — Graduated fines and demerit points
laws.fullDescription: New South Wales uses a graduated speeding penalty system. Speeding 30+ km/h over limit: immediate licence suspension and fine from $1,200+. Excessive speed (typically 30+ km/h over limit) results in immediate licence suspension. Demerit points accumulate against your licence.
laws.penalty: 30+ km/h: $1,202 fine + 6 demerit points + immediate suspension. 45+ km/h: $2,530 + licence suspension.
exceptions: School zone and construction zone penalties typically doubled
Learner/P-plate drivers face lower demerit point thresholds
Demerit point scheme — accumulating points leads to suspension
laws.sourceLabel: New South Wales Road Rules / Fines

quiz.q: What typically happens in New South Wales if a driver is caught travelling more than 30 km/h over the speed limit?
options: Immediate licence suspension plus a substantial fine
quiz.explanation: In New South Wales, driving 30+ km/h over the speed limit typically results in immediate licence suspension and a large fine. The exact threshold varies by state.

laws.title: Age of Majority — 18 in New South Wales
laws.subtitle: Minors (Property and Contracts) Act 1970 (NSW) — Age of majority is 18
laws.fullDescription: The age of majority in New South Wales (and all Australian states/territories) is 18. At 18, individuals gain full legal capacity — they can vote, enter binding contracts, consume alcohol, and are tried as adults in criminal proceedings. NSW follows the national standard of 18 as the age of majority.
laws.penalty: Minors' contracts are generally voidable at their option.
exceptions: Children may have some legal standing earlier (e.g., 16 for employment contracts)
Gillick competence allows younger minors to make some medical decisions
Age of criminal responsibility is 10 federally (proposed reform to raise)

quiz.q: What is the age of majority in all Australian states and territories?
quiz.explanation: The age of majority is 18 across all Australian states and territories — the age at which full legal rights and responsibilities attach.

laws.title: Voting — Compulsory in Australia
laws.subtitle: Commonwealth Electoral Act 1918 (Cth) — Voting is compulsory
laws.fullDescription: Australia has compulsory voting for all citizens aged 18+ in federal elections (since 1924) and New South Wales also has compulsory voting in state elections. Failure to vote without a valid reason results in a fine. Australia is one of fewer than 25 countries globally with compulsory voting.
laws.penalty: Failure to vote without valid reason: $20 administrative penalty (federal), rising to court fine if not paid.
exceptions: Valid excuses: illness, remote location, religious objection (with evidence)
Overseas Australians on the electoral roll must enrol
Informal (blank/spoiled) voting is legally permitted

quiz.q: Is voting compulsory for eligible Australian citizens?
options: Yes — voting is compulsory for citizens 18+
Only for federal elections, not state
Only if you are enrolled to vote
quiz.explanation: Voting is compulsory for all enrolled Australian citizens 18+. Australia has had compulsory voting since 1924 — one of the few countries in the world to mandate it.

laws.title: Jury Duty — Compulsory for Eligible Citizens
laws.subtitle: Jury Act 1977 (NSW) — Random selection from electoral roll
laws.fullDescription: New South Wales: Eligible NSW residents are randomly selected from the electoral roll for jury service. Certain professions and those with serious convictions are disqualified. Jurors are selected randomly from the electoral roll. Serving on a jury is a legal obligation for eligible citizens.
laws.penalty: Failure to attend without excuse: fines or contempt of court.
exceptions: Certain professions may be excluded (judges, lawyers, police, medical professionals in some states)
Genuine hardship may justify excuse or deferral
Non-citizens not on the electoral roll are not eligible
laws.sourceLabel: New South Wales Jury Act

quiz.q: How are jurors selected in Australia?
quiz.explanation: Jurors in Australia are selected randomly from the electoral roll — the register of enrolled voters.

laws.title: Mandatory Reporting — Child Abuse & Neglect
laws.subtitle: Children and Young Persons (Care and Protection) Act 1998 (NSW) s. 27 — Mandatory reporters must report
laws.fullDescription: New South Wales: NSW is unique — all adults (not just professionals) must report if they suspect a child is at risk of significant harm. Mandatory reporters have additional obligations. Mandatory reporters are required to report to child protection authorities (not police) when they form a reasonable suspicion of child abuse or neglect.
laws.penalty: Failure to report (mandatory reporters): fine.
exceptions: Good faith reports protected from civil/criminal liability
Report may be made anonymously
Does not require certainty — reasonable belief/suspicion is sufficient
laws.sourceLabel: New South Wales Child Protection Legislation

quiz.q: Who is generally required to make mandatory reports of child abuse in Australian states?
options: Specified professionals (teachers, doctors, social workers, etc.) — varies by state
quiz.explanation: Most Australian states mandate specific professionals (teachers, doctors, nurses, social workers, etc.) to report suspected child abuse. Some states (e.g., NSW) extend this to all adults.

laws.title: Age of Consent — 16 in New South Wales
laws.subtitle: Crimes Act 1900 (NSW) s. 66C — Age of consent: 16
laws.fullDescription: The age of consent in New South Wales is 16. NSW age of consent is 16 for most purposes. Age raised to 18 where there is a relationship of authority or special care. Special rules apply where there is a relationship of authority/trust (age raised to 18). Child abuse material offences apply regardless of consent.
laws.penalty: Sexual activity with persons under the age of consent: serious criminal offence with substantial imprisonment terms.
exceptions: Close-in-age provisions exist in some states
No exception for positions of trust — age raised to 18
Marriage does not lower the age of consent (minimum marriage age is 18 federally)

quiz.q: What is the age of consent in New South Wales?
quiz.explanation: The age of consent in New South Wales is 16. Sexual activity with persons under this age is a serious criminal offence.

laws.title: Age of Criminal Responsibility — Doli Incapax
laws.subtitle: Criminal Code (federal proposal: raise to 14) — Currently 10
laws.fullDescription: Australia's age of criminal responsibility is 10 — children aged 10 or older can be charged with criminal offences. Children 10–13 have a rebuttable presumption (doli incapax) that they did not understand their actions were seriously wrong. New South Wales: NSW has the national age of 10. The NSW Law Reform Commission has recommended raising it to 14. A federal review has proposed raising the minimum age to 14, in line with international standards.
laws.penalty: Children in conflict with the law are dealt with in Children's/Youth Courts.
exceptions: Doli incapax presumption (ages 10–13): prosecution must rebut
Children's Courts aim for rehabilitation over punishment
Detention is a last resort for juveniles
laws.sourceLabel: New South Wales Youth Justice / Crimes Act

quiz.q: What is the current minimum age of criminal responsibility in Australian states?
quiz.explanation: The minimum age of criminal responsibility in Australia is 10 — one of the lowest in the world. Advocacy groups and a federal review have called for it to be raised to 14.

laws.title: Youth Curfew Laws — New South Wales
laws.subtitle: No general curfew law — No general youth curfew
laws.fullDescription: New South Wales: NSW has no general youth curfew law. Courts may impose curfew conditions on individual young offenders. Curfew orders may also be imposed by courts as conditions of bail or supervised release for individual young offenders.
laws.penalty: Curfew breach: police may take minor home; court consequences for ordered curfews.
exceptions: Court-ordered curfews for individual young offenders
Police may return young people home for welfare reasons
Family law curfew conditions may exist in parenting orders
laws.sourceLabel: New South Wales / Local Law

quiz.q: Do Australian states have widespread general youth curfew laws?
options: Yes — all states have 10 PM curfews
Generally no — courts impose individual curfews; few general laws
quiz.explanation: Most Australian states do not have broad general youth curfew laws. Courts impose curfews on individual young offenders as conditions of bail/supervision.

laws.title: Corporal Punishment — Schools Banned; Home Restricted
laws.subtitle: Crimes Act 1900 (NSW) s. 61AA — Schools: banned; parents: limited defence
laws.fullDescription: Corporal punishment in all Australian schools (government and private) is banned. New South Wales: Corporal punishment in NSW schools is banned. laws.penalty: Excessive physical punishment of children: assault charges.
exceptions: 'Lawful correction' defence for parents only — schools have no defence
Must be reasonable and moderate — no implements, not to head/face
ACT has prohibited all corporal punishment including by parents

quiz.q: Is corporal punishment (physical discipline) permitted in Australian schools?
options: No — banned in all schools (government and private)
quiz.explanation: Corporal punishment is banned in all Australian schools. Parents retain a limited 'lawful correction' defence for home discipline, though this varies by state.

laws.title: Home Schooling — Regulated in New South Wales
laws.subtitle: Education Act 1990 (NSW) — Registration required
laws.fullDescription: New South Wales: NSW permits home education. Parents must register with the NSW Education Standards Authority (NESA) and comply with curriculum requirements. All children of compulsory school age must be enrolled in a registered school or approved home education program.
laws.penalty: Failure to register while home educating: fine.
exceptions: Parents need not be qualified teachers in most states
Curriculum requirements vary by state
Regular assessments or reporting may be required

quiz.q: Is home education legal in New South Wales?
options: Illegal — all children must attend school
Legal but requires registration and compliance with curriculum requirements
quiz.explanation: Home education is legal in New South Wales but requires registration with NESA and curriculum compliance.

laws.title: 'No Jab, No Pay' & 'No Jab, No Play'
laws.subtitle: Family Assistance Legislation Amendment Act 2015 + state laws
laws.fullDescription: Australia's 'No Jab, No Pay' federal policy (2016) ties family payments to children's vaccination status — unvaccinated children of parents who refuse vaccination lose access to childcare benefit/rebate and Family Tax Benefit supplements. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children and children in remote areas have separate pathways

options: A police fine for not vaccinating
A policy requiring vaccination to enter Australia
Federal family payments tied to children's vaccination status
quiz.explanation: 'No Jab, No Pay' links federal family payments to vaccination compliance. Conscientious objection exemptions were removed in 2016 — only medical exemptions remain.

laws.title: Abortion — Legal in New South Wales
laws.subtitle: Abortion Law Reform Act 2019 (NSW) — Decriminalised and regulated
laws.fullDescription: Abortion has been decriminalised across all Australian states and territories. New South Wales: NSW decriminalised abortion in 2019. Abortion is legal to 22 weeks; after 22 weeks two practitioners must agree it is appropriate in the circumstances. Safe access zones apply around clinics. Safe access zones around clinics in most states

quiz.q: Is abortion legal in all Australian states and territories?
options: No — still illegal in some states
Yes — decriminalised and regulated in all states and territories
Only federally — states cannot legalise it
quiz.explanation: Abortion has been fully decriminalised across all Australian states and territories — the last to do so was South Australia in 2021.

laws.title: Death Penalty — Abolished in Australia
laws.subtitle: Death Penalty Abolition Act 1973 (Cth) — Federally abolished
laws.fullDescription: Australia abolished the death penalty federally in 1973 and in all states by 1985. The last execution in Australia was Ronald Ryan in Victoria in 1967. Australia also will not extradite individuals to face the death penalty without assurances. NSW (and all Australian states) cannot impose capital punishment following federal abolition in 1973.

Federal abolition prevents any state from reintroducing it
Life imprisonment is the maximum penalty

quiz.q: When was the death penalty abolished at the federal level in Australia?
quiz.explanation: The Death Penalty Abolition Act 1973 abolished capital punishment for all federal offences. All states followed — Queensland last in 1922, but the last execution was Ronald Ryan in Victoria in 1967.

laws.title: Voluntary Assisted Dying (VAD) — Legal since 2023
laws.subtitle: Voluntary Assisted Dying Act 2022 (NSW) — Legal for terminally ill adults since November 2023
laws.fullDescription: New South Wales: NSW passed its Voluntary Assisted Dying Act in 2022, commencing November 2023. Eligible adults with a terminal illness expected to cause death within 12 months (6 months for most) may request VAD. Only in hospitals, not at home
quiz.explanation: NSW legalised Voluntary Assisted Dying in 2022 (commenced 2023). All Australian states and territories now have VAD legislation.

laws.title: Drug Offences — New South Wales

laws.fullDescription: Drug offences in New South Wales are governed by both state legislation and the Commonwealth Criminal Code. NSW has a cannabis cautioning program for minor possession. Court-ordered treatment as alternative to imprisonment for addicted offenders

options: May be diverted to a caution or education program

laws.title: Proceeds of Crime — Confiscation
laws.subtitle: Proceeds of Crime Act 2002 (Cth) + Criminal Assets Recovery Act 1990 (NSW)
laws.fullDescription: Australia has comprehensive proceeds of crime legislation at both federal and state levels. Third parties with legitimate interest may claim

quiz.q: Can Australian authorities seize assets before a criminal conviction?
options: No — only after a civil court order
Yes — assets can be restrained before conviction in most states
Only the federal government can seize assets
quiz.explanation: Australian proceeds of crime legislation allows assets to be restrained (frozen) before conviction. Post-conviction forfeiture and (in some states) civil forfeiture without conviction are also available.

laws.title: Spent Convictions — Rehabilitation of Offenders
laws.subtitle: Criminal Records Act 1991 (NSW) — Spent convictions after waiting period
laws.fullDescription: New South Wales: NSW convictions become spent after a 10-year crime-free period (3 years for children). Certain serious offences are ineligible. options: It is erased from all records completely
It need not be disclosed in most circumstances after a crime-free waiting period
It can only be accessed by police

laws.title: Solitary Confinement / Segregation in Prisons
laws.subtitle: Crimes (Administration of Sentences) Act 1999 (NSW) — Segregation permitted with oversight
laws.fullDescription: New South Wales: NSW allows segregation in exceptional circumstances. The Inspector of Custodial Services provides oversight. laws.title: Private Prisons — New South Wales

laws.fullDescription: New South Wales: NSW operates both public and private prisons. Parklea Correctional Centre and others are privately managed by Serco and MTC under government contracts. Australia has a significant private prison sector compared to many comparable nations.

laws.title: Police Body-Worn Cameras — New South Wales
laws.subtitle: Deployed — NSW Police has body-worn video

laws.title: Police Use of Force — New South Wales

laws.fullDescription: New South Wales police use-of-force is governed by Law Enforcement (Powers and Responsibilities) Act 2002 (NSW) and policy frameworks. Force must be necessary and proportionate. Complaints to police oversight body

laws.title: Domestic Violence Disclosure Scheme — New South Wales

Proactive disclosure also possible where police identify risk

Only victims can access this information

laws.title: Racial Vilification & Hate Speech Laws

Only government actions based on race

laws.title: Family Violence — Protection Orders & Criminal Offences

laws.fullDescription: New South Wales: NSW provides Apprehended Domestic Violence Orders (ADVOs) for protection. NSW Police have power to issue provisional orders immediately. Only if the victim is a child
quiz.explanation: Australian prosecutors can and often do proceed with domestic violence charges independent of the victim's cooperation — recognising that victims may be pressured or fear reprisal.

laws.title: Stalking / Cyberstalking — Criminal Offence
laws.subtitle: Crimes (Domestic and Personal Violence) Act 2007 (NSW) s. 13 — Stalking offences with significant penalties
laws.fullDescription: New South Wales: NSW's stalking and intimidation offence covers physical and online conduct intended to cause fear. Maximum 5 years imprisonment. Cyberstalking (online harassment, surveillance) is also a serious offence. Protection orders are available through both civil and criminal processes.
laws.penalty: Up to 5 years imprisonment.
exceptions: Restraining orders/protection orders available
Apprehended violence orders (AVOs) in NSW provide civil protection
Online/cyber harassment now explicitly covered in most state laws
laws.sourceLabel: New South Wales Stalking / Harassment Laws

quiz.q: Is cyberstalking (online harassment and surveillance) a criminal offence in Australia?
options: No — only physical stalking is criminal
Yes — covered under stalking/harassment laws in all states
Only if it involves explicit threats
quiz.explanation: Cyberstalking and online harassment are criminal offences across all Australian states and territories, recognising the serious harm caused by digital-based stalking.

laws.title: Privacy — Privacy Act 1988 (Federal)
laws.subtitle: Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) — Australian Privacy Principles (APPs)
laws.fullDescription: The federal Privacy Act 1988 governs how organisations handle personal information through 13 Australian Privacy Principles (APPs). The Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC) oversees compliance. New South Wales: NSW organisations are covered by the federal Privacy Act 1988. NSW Health Privacy Act applies to health information held by NSW Health. The Privacy Act is currently under reform to strengthen protections.
laws.penalty: Serious/repeated privacy breaches: up to $50 million penalty (organisations) under 2023 reforms.
exceptions: Small businesses (under $3M turnover) generally exempt
Health service providers — all covered regardless of size
Notifiable Data Breaches (NDB) scheme: breaches likely to cause serious harm must be reported
laws.sourceLabel: Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC)

quiz.q: Which body enforces the Australian Privacy Principles?
options: Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC)
quiz.explanation: The OAIC oversees compliance with the Privacy Act 1988 and Australian Privacy Principles, investigating complaints and taking regulatory action.

laws.title: Online Safety — eSafety Commissioner
laws.subtitle: Online Safety Act 2021 (Cth) — eSafety Commissioner
laws.fullDescription: Australia's Online Safety Act 2021 established the eSafety Commissioner with powers to order removal of online content including cyberbullying material targeting children, non-consensual intimate images, and seriously harmful online content. New South Wales residents benefit from this federal framework. NSW residents can contact the eSafety Commissioner for cyberbullying or NCII (non-consensual intimate images) removal.
laws.penalty: Platform non-compliance with eSafety notices: fines up to $550,000/day.
exceptions: eSafety can order removal of NCII (non-consensual intimate images) within 24 hours
Basic Online Safety Expectations require platforms to tackle harmful content
Age verification for online pornography under consultation
laws.sourceLabel: eSafety Commissioner / Online Safety Act 2021

quiz.q: What power does Australia's eSafety Commissioner have?
options: Issue removal notices to platforms for harmful content
quiz.explanation: The eSafety Commissioner can issue notices requiring social media platforms to remove harmful content — including cyberbullying, NCII, and seriously harmful material. Non-compliance attracts significant fines.

laws.title: Environmental Protection — EPBC Act
laws.subtitle: Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act 1999 (Cth) + state laws
laws.fullDescription: Australia's EPBC Act protects matters of national environmental significance — threatened species, World Heritage areas, Ramsar wetlands, and more. New South Wales: NSW's Environment Protection Authority (EPA) enforces state environmental laws. NSW has a Biodiversity Conservation Act 2016 replacing previous threatened species legislation. State environmental agencies regulate local pollution, land clearing, and development.
laws.penalty: EPBC breaches: civil penalties up to $22.5M for companies; criminal prosecution for serious offences.
exceptions: Referral required for significant impacts on EPBC matters
Indigenous protected areas recognised
Climate change listed as a key threatening process under review
laws.sourceLabel: EPBC Act / New South Wales Environment Protection

quiz.q: What does Australia's EPBC Act protect?
options: Matters of national environmental significance (threatened species, World Heritage, Ramsar wetlands, etc.)
quiz.explanation: The EPBC Act protects matters of national environmental significance, including threatened species and communities, World Heritage areas, Ramsar wetlands, and migratory species.

laws.title: Renewable Energy — New South Wales's Grid
laws.subtitle: Electricity Infrastructure Investment Act 2020 (NSW) — Renewables rapidly expanding
laws.fullDescription: New South Wales: NSW is investing heavily in renewable energy. The NSW Electricity Investment Road Map targets 12 GW of new renewable energy by 2030. Renewable penetration growing rapidly from coal baseline. Australia's federal Renewable Energy Target (RET) has driven significant investment in wind and solar. Australia ranks among the world's fastest-growing solar markets per capita.
laws.penalty: N/A — renewable energy targets are policy/regulatory.
exceptions: Rooftop solar very popular — Australia has highest per-capita uptake globally
Feed-in tariffs vary by state
Large-scale renewables expanding rapidly
laws.sourceLabel: New South Wales Energy Policy

quiz.q: Approximately what percentage of New South Wales's electricity comes from renewable sources?
quiz.explanation: As of 2024, approximately ~40% of New South Wales's electricity comes from renewable sources. Renewables are rapidly expanding across all states.

laws.title: Single-Use Plastics — Bans Across Australia
laws.subtitle: Plastic Reduction and Circular Economy Act 2021 (NSW) — Phased bans from 2022
laws.fullDescription: All Australian states and territories have banned lightweight single-use plastic bags. New South Wales: NSW banned lightweight single-use plastic bags, single-use straws, cutlery, and polystyrene food containers from November 2022, with further items from 2023. Additional bans on straws, cutlery, and food containers are being rolled out.
laws.penalty: Supply of banned items: fines up to $11,000 (individual) / $55,500 (corporation).
exceptions: Reusable bags, paper bags, and heavy-duty bags permitted
Medical/healthcare plastic items exempt
Dry cleaning bags and some specialty bags may be exempt
laws.sourceLabel: New South Wales Environment Protection

quiz.q: Are single-use lightweight plastic bags banned in Australia?
options: Yes — banned in all states and territories
Only in supermarkets, not in general retail
quiz.explanation: All Australian states and territories have banned lightweight single-use plastic bags. The bans have been progressively extended to other single-use plastics.

laws.title: Container Deposit Scheme (CDS) — New South Wales
laws.subtitle: Waste Avoidance and Resource Recovery Act 2001 (NSW) — Return and Earn CDS
laws.fullDescription: New South Wales: NSW operates the Return and Earn Container Deposit Scheme. A 10¢ refund is available for eligible beverage containers returned to reverse vending machines or collection depots. The 10¢ deposit incentivises return and recycling of eligible beverage containers.
laws.penalty: Operating an unauthorised return point: fine.
exceptions: Not all containers eligible — alcohol over certain sizes may differ
Network of return points and reverse vending machines
Charities often benefit from donated refund points
laws.sourceLabel: New South Wales CDS

quiz.q: What is the refund amount per eligible container returned under New South Wales's Container Deposit Scheme?
quiz.explanation: New South Wales's CDS provides a 10 cent refund per eligible container returned — incentivising recycling and reducing litter.

laws.title: Animal Cruelty — Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act
laws.subtitle: Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act 1979 (NSW) — Cruelty and neglect prohibited
laws.fullDescription: New South Wales's NSW's POCTA Act prohibits cruelty and neglect. RSPCA NSW and Animal Welfare League enforce. Penalty notices and prosecution available. RSPCA and inspectors have enforcement powers. Penalties have increased significantly in recent years.
laws.penalty: Up to $22,000 fine (individual) / $110,000 (corporation) and 5 years imprisonment.
exceptions: Farming practices under approved codes of practice may be exempt
Veterinary procedures
Pest animal control under approved methods
laws.sourceLabel: New South Wales RSPCA / Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act

quiz.q: Which organisation primarily enforces animal cruelty laws in Australian states?
quiz.explanation: The RSPCA (Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals) is the primary enforcement body for animal cruelty legislation in Australian states and territories.

laws.title: Exotic & Dangerous Animals as Pets
laws.subtitle: Biodiversity Conservation Act 2016 (NSW) / Biosecurity Act 2015 — Strict regulation; many species prohibited
laws.fullDescription: New South Wales: NSW prohibits keeping most wildlife and many exotic species. Prohibited invasive animals (foxes, rabbits, cats in some areas) must not be kept. Native birds, reptiles, and mammals require a licence. The importation of most exotic animals is strictly controlled under federal law (EPBC Act, Customs Act). Native wildlife cannot be kept as pets without a permit in most states.
laws.penalty: Keeping prohibited species: up to $44,000 fine.
exceptions: Licensed wildlife sanctuaries and research facilities
Some native species permitted as pets in specific states (e.g., sugar gliders in some)
Zoos under strict licensing
laws.sourceLabel: New South Wales Biodiversity Conservation / EPBC Act

quiz.q: Can most exotic animals (e.g., lions, tigers, primates) be kept as pets in Australia?
options: Yes — if bought from a licenced dealer
No — most exotic and many native animals are prohibited without special permits
quiz.explanation: Australia's strict biosecurity laws and wildlife protection legislation prohibit most exotic animals as pets. Even many native species require permits to keep.

laws.title: Fireworks — Strictly Regulated
laws.subtitle: Explosives Act 2003 (NSW) — Consumer fireworks heavily restricted
laws.fullDescription: New South Wales: NSW bans consumer fireworks. Only licensed pyrotechnicians may discharge fireworks. Council-authorised public displays only. Unlike many countries, most Australian states ban consumer fireworks entirely — professional licensed operators only.
laws.penalty: Illegal fireworks: up to $22,000 fine.
exceptions: Professional fireworks operators require licence
Approved public displays only
NT has the most permissive laws — Territory Day (1 July) allows limited personal use
laws.sourceLabel: New South Wales Explosives / Dangerous Goods Act

quiz.q: Which Australian territory uniquely allows limited personal fireworks use on Territory Day (1 July)?
quiz.explanation: The Northern Territory uniquely permits limited personal fireworks use on Territory Day (1 July). Other states and the ACT generally ban consumer fireworks — professional displays only.

laws.title: Gambling — State-Regulated
laws.subtitle: Casino Control Act 1992 / Liquor and Gaming NSW — Regulated by NSW Independent Casino Commission / Liquor and Gaming NSW
laws.fullDescription: Gambling in New South Wales is regulated by NSW Independent Casino Commission / Liquor and Gaming NSW. NSW has The Star casino in Sydney. Poker machines (pokies) are widely available in pubs and clubs — NSW has more pokies than any other state. Responsible gambling measures mandated. Australia has one of the highest gambling expenditures per capita in the world — driven largely by electronic gaming machines (pokies).
laws.penalty: Operating unlicensed gambling: significant criminal penalties.
exceptions: Online gambling regulated by federal Interactive Gambling Act 2001
In-play sports betting online is prohibited (federal)
Problem gambling: mandatory self-exclusion schemes in all states
laws.sourceLabel: NSW Independent Casino Commission / Liquor and Gaming NSW

quiz.q: Australia has one of the world's highest gambling expenditures per capita, driven primarily by what type of gambling device?
quiz.explanation: Australia has one of the world's highest gambling losses per adult, driven largely by electronic gaming machines (pokies). There are approximately 200,000 poker machines across Australia.

laws.title: Online Gambling — Interactive Gambling Act 2001 (Cth)
laws.subtitle: Interactive Gambling Act 2001 (Cth) — In-play betting banned online
laws.fullDescription: The federal Interactive Gambling Act 2001 (IGA) regulates online gambling in Australia. It prohibits Australian-based operators from offering online casino games (pokies, roulette, blackjack) to Australians. In-play (live) sports betting online is also prohibited. NSW residents using VPNs to access offshore online casinos violate the intent of the IGA. Licensed Australian sports betting websites are permitted for pre-game wagering.
laws.penalty: Unlicensed online gambling provision: up to $1.1M per day (companies).
exceptions: Sports betting licensed in each state — pre-game online permitted
Fantasy sports with prizes may be exempt
VPNs to access foreign gambling sites violate the spirit of the IGA
laws.sourceLabel: Interactive Gambling Act 2001

quiz.q: What does Australia's Interactive Gambling Act prohibit?
options: All online betting including sports wagering
Online casino games and in-play sports betting for Australian users
quiz.explanation: The IGA prohibits online casino-style games (pokies, roulette) and in-play sports betting for Australians, while allowing licensed sports betting platforms for pre-game wagering.

laws.title: Right to Repair — Emerging in Australia
laws.subtitle: Australian Consumer Law (ACL) — ACL guarantees apply; no specific right-to-repair law
laws.fullDescription: New South Wales: NSW applies the federal Australian Consumer Law, which provides strong repair/replacement/refund rights for faulty goods. No specific right-to-repair legislation exists at state level. Australia's Productivity Commission recommended introducing a right to repair in 2021. Consumer guarantees under the Australian Consumer Law (ACL) provide some repair rights.
laws.penalty: N/A — emerging policy area.
exceptions: Australian Consumer Law guarantees repair/replacement/refund for major failures
Competition and Consumer Act 2010 prohibits anti-competitive repair restrictions
Statutory warranty rights stronger than some overseas jurisdictions
laws.sourceLabel: ACCC / New South Wales / Federal

quiz.q: What does Australia's Consumer Law (ACL) guarantee for products with major failures?
options: A repair, replacement, or refund at the consumer's choice
quiz.explanation: Under the ACL, consumers are entitled to choose between a repair, replacement, or refund for products with major failures — a foundation for right-to-repair protections.

laws.title: LGBTQ+ Rights — New South Wales
laws.subtitle: Sex Discrimination Act 1984 (Cth) + Anti-Discrimination Act 1977 (NSW) — Comprehensive protections
laws.fullDescription: Australia has federal anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ+ people under the Sex Discrimination Act 1984 (amended 2013 to include sexual orientation and gender identity). Same-sex marriage has been legal since December 9, 2017 (Marriage Amendment Act 2017). New South Wales: NSW's Anti-Discrimination Act protects against discrimination based on homosexuality (since 1982) and gender identity (since 1996). Conversion practices are prohibited in NSW (Conversion Practices Prohibition Act 2024). Conversion practices are banned in several states.
laws.penalty: Discrimination on basis of sexual orientation or gender identity: complaints to AHRC or state tribunal.
exceptions: Conversion practices banned in NSW, Victoria, Queensland, ACT, SA, and WA
Religious exemptions in employment by religious bodies remain contested
Trans people can change legal gender on documents (federal and state reforms)
laws.sourceLabel: Sex Discrimination Act / New South Wales

quiz.q: When did same-sex marriage become legal across Australia?
quiz.explanation: Same-sex marriage became legal in Australia on 9 December 2017, following the voluntary postal survey in which 61.6% voted 'yes', and the subsequent Marriage Amendment Act 2017.

laws.title: Driver's Licence — Visitors & New Residents
laws.subtitle: Foreign licences valid for 3 months; convert after taking up residency
laws.fullDescription: Overseas visitors may drive in NSW on their foreign licence for up to 3 months from the date of arrival, provided the licence is in English or accompanied by an accredited English translation or International Driving Permit (IDP). After 3 months, new NSW residents must convert their overseas licence to an NSW licence at a Service NSW centre. Some countries qualify for direct conversion without a driving test.
laws.penalty: Driving without a valid licence: fine up to $2,200; vehicle may be impounded
exceptions: Diplomatic personnel with valid diplomatic IDs
Members of visiting armed forces under bilateral agreements
Short-term tourists within the 3-month window with valid foreign licence
laws.sourceLabel: Transport for NSW / Austroads

quiz.q: How long may an overseas visitor drive in New South Wales on their foreign driver's licence?
quiz.explanation: Overseas visitors may drive in New South Wales on a valid foreign licence for up to 3 months from arrival. After that, new residents must convert to a NSW licence.

laws.title: Hunting & Fishing — Interstate & Overseas Visitors
laws.subtitle: Same licences apply to all — no 'non-resident' surcharge in NSW
laws.fullDescription: NSW applies the same licence fees and rules to interstate visitors as to residents. A NSW Recreational Fishing Fee applies to anyone fishing in NSW waters (with limited exemptions). Australian states generally do not apply higher fees for interstate visitors, unlike some US states. Always check species-specific rules, bag limits, and seasonal restrictions before fishing or hunting.
laws.penalty: Fishing without a licence: fine up to $2,200; hunting without a Game Hunting Licence: fine up to $22,000
exceptions: Indigenous Australians exercising native title or traditional rights
Children under minimum age thresholds
Activities on private land with landowner permission (for some species)
laws.sourceLabel: New South Wales Fisheries / DPI

quiz.q: Do interstate visitors pay higher hunting or fishing licence fees in New South Wales compared to residents?
options: No — same fees apply to all
Only overseas visitors pay a higher fee
quiz.explanation: Unlike some US states, Australian states do not generally impose higher 'non-resident' licence fees. Interstate visitors pay the same as New South Wales residents.

laws.title: Drink Driving Enforcement — Mid-Range & High-Range BAC
laws.subtitle: 0.05% general limit; heavier penalties above 0.08% and 0.15%
laws.fullDescription: All Australian states share the 0.05% BAC limit for fully licensed drivers. New South Wales uses tiered penalties: low-range (0.05–0.079%), mid-range (0.08–0.149%), and high-range (≥0.15%). NSW conducts more than 5 million random breath tests per year — among the highest rates in Australia. Mobile RBT units operate 24/7. Mid-range (0.08–0.15) and high-range (≥0.15) BAC attract heavier penalties including mandatory interlock. Random Breath Testing (RBT) is conducted without suspicion of impairment — any driver can be stopped.
laws.penalty: Low-range: $561 fine + 3 demerit points; Mid-range: $2,200 fine, 12-month disqualification (first offence); mandatory alcohol interlock on licence restoration; High-range: $3,300 fine, 3-year disqualification (first offence); mandatory interlock
exceptions: Medical conditions causing false positives are subject to challenge
Mouth alcohol (mouthwash) dissipates — 15-minute observation period before test
laws.sourceLabel: New South Wales Roads Authority / Police

quiz.q: In Australia, which blood alcohol level is generally classed as 'high-range' drink driving?
quiz.explanation: Australia's high-range drink driving threshold is ≥0.15% BAC. This attracts the severest automatic penalties including long disqualifications and mandatory alcohol interlocks.

laws.title: Mandatory Seat Belts — All Occupants
laws.subtitle: Every person in a moving vehicle must be correctly restrained
laws.fullDescription: All occupants must wear an approved seatbelt at all times. Children must be restrained in an approved child seat appropriate for their age/size. The driver is responsible for ensuring passengers under 16 are correctly restrained. Seat belts have been compulsory in Australia since 1971 (VIC was the first jurisdiction in the world to make them mandatory, in 1970). Child restraint rules: rear-facing for infants, forward-facing with harness for toddlers, booster seats for children up to approximately 145cm.
laws.penalty: $387 fine + 3 demerit points per unbelted occupant (driver responsible for passengers under 16)
exceptions: Reversing a vehicle at low speed on private property
Medical exemption certificate holders
Emergency services personnel performing specific operational duties
laws.sourceLabel: New South Wales Road Rules

quiz.q: Who was the first jurisdiction in the world to make seat belts compulsory?
quiz.explanation: Victoria, Australia introduced mandatory seat belt laws in 1970 — the first jurisdiction in the world to do so. All Australian states now require all occupants to be belted.

laws.title: School Zone Speed Limit — 40 km/h
laws.subtitle: Reduced speed applies during school drop-off and pick-up times
laws.fullDescription: School zones in New South Wales require drivers to slow to 40 km/h during active school hours. School zones operate at 40 km/h on school days between 8:00–9:30 am and 2:30–4:00 pm. Electronic variable speed signs indicate active zones. "Safe Stopping" zones prohibit parking adjacent to school zones during these hours. School zones are typically marked with fluorescent yellow/green signs and, in many locations, flashing amber lights to indicate when the limit is active. Increased demerit points often apply during double-demerit periods.
laws.penalty: $457 fine + 5 demerit points (double demerit periods apply on public holidays)
exceptions: Vehicles responding to emergency calls (sirens/lights active)
